summary: Specifies version 4 of the Network File System protocol, a distributed file system that builds on NFS versions 2 and 3. It folds in file locking and mounting and adds features such as stronger security and better performance over the internet. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 7530.

plainLanguage.summary: You can keep your files on one computer and open them from another as if they were right there. This memo describes the fourth version of the system that does that.

questions: how does nfs file locking work
what is the nfsv4 compound procedure
subtitle: The fourth version of the Network File System: stateful, secure by design, and built to work across the Internet.

tldr.problem: Earlier NFS versions needed side protocols for mounting and locking, relied on trusting client machines, and were chatty over high-latency links.
tldr.mechanism: NFS version 4 runs everything through two RPC procedures, NULL and COMPOUND, folds in mounting and byte-range locking with server-held, lease-based state, mandates RPCSEC_GSS security, and lets servers delegate files to clients for local caching.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3530 replaced RFC 3010 as the definition of NFS version 4, and was itself obsoleted by RFC 7530.

today: RFC 3530 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3010 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 7530, which is now the definition of NFS version 4. It remains useful as the earlier specification of minor version zero.

sections.title: Goals and Heritage
sections.content:
NFS version 4 is a distributed filesystem protocol that descends from NFS version 2 (RFC 1094) and version 3 (RFC 1813). It keeps their core traits: easy recovery, independence from transport, operating system and filesystem, simplicity and good performance. Unlike earlier versions, it supports ordinary file access while also integrating file locking and the mount protocol.

The RFC lists four goals: good access and performance on the Internet (it is meant to pass firewalls easily, perform well when latency is high and bandwidth low, and scale to very many clients per server), strong security with negotiation built in, good cross-platform interoperability, and extensibility without breaking backward compatibility.

This document replaces RFC 3010. The changes came from implementation experience; most fixed errors or situations where the earlier definition was untenable. Examples include a new open_owner4 identifier for POSIX clients, a limit on the size of opaque identifiers, and a new mounted_on_fileid attribute. The XDR definitions in Section 18 are authoritative wherever the explanatory text disagrees with them.
sections.plainLanguage: NFS lets one computer use files that live on another, like borrowing books from a library across town. Version 4 tries to make that safer, faster and easier to run across the Internet.

sections.title: The COMPOUND Procedure
sections.content:
NFS version 4 has only two RPC procedures, NULL and COMPOUND. Everything else is an operation packed inside a COMPOUND request. A client can therefore chain several steps in one round trip. The RFC's example is reading a file with no earlier contact by combining LOOKUP, OPEN and READ in a single request, which was not possible before.

The server evaluates the operations in order. There is no logical AND or OR. When an operation returns a non-zero status, evaluation stops and the results so far are returned. This holds even for non-error conditions such as NFS4ERR_SAME. Operations are not atomic as a group, so the client is responsible for recovering from a partly completed compound request, and should avoid overly complex ones.

Operations share an execution context holding a current filehandle and a saved filehandle. Most operations act on the current one; the saved one is temporary storage and the second operand of RENAME and LINK. Operations that modify the filesystem are synchronous: once one succeeds, its data is on stable storage, except for WRITE with the UNSTABLE option. Operation values 0 and 1 are not defined, and 2 is reserved for minor versioning.

The server also calls back into the client through a separate NFS4_CALLBACK program with CB_NULL and CB_COMPOUND. The client chooses its program number in the transient range and tells the server the program and port during SETCLIENTID.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of making a separate trip to the store for each item, you hand over one shopping list and the shop works through it in order. If one item is not available, it stops and tells you how far it got.

sections.title: RPC, Transports and Security
sections.content:
NFS version 4 is an RPC version 2 application using XDR. The RPCSEC_GSS security flavor (RFC 2203) MUST be used to deliver the stronger security. Other flavors such as AUTH_NONE, AUTH_SYS and AUTH_DH MAY be implemented too. Choosing RPCSEC_GSS means choosing a mechanism, a quality of protection and a service (authentication, integrity or privacy), which the RFC calls a security triple.

Implementations MUST support three GSS-API mechanisms: Kerberos V5 (RFC 1964), LIPKEY and SPKM-3 (both from RFC 2847). LIPKEY passes a user name and password through an SPKM-3 channel. SPKM-3 is mandatory as well to cover clients that are anonymous or already hold a certificate. The RFC warns that 56-bit DES, used with Kerberos here, is no longer state of the art, and urges a move to AES once available.

The registered port 2049 should be the default, so clients need not use RPC binding and NFS can pass firewalls. Over IP, transports MUST be IETF-approved congestion-controlled protocols such as TCP and SCTP, and implementations MUST support TCP, ideally with persistent connections. On a reliable transport a server MUST NOT silently drop a request, so a client MUST NOT retry unless the connection broke or the procedure is NULL. A NULL call is the suggested way to probe a connection.

Because a server can offer different security on different parts of its name space, the new SECINFO operation lets the client ask which triple to use for a given filehandle. A server answers a mismatch with NFS4ERR_WRONGSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you may enter the library, the librarian checks your card in a way nobody can fake. The two sides also agree on the strongest lock both of them support.

sections.title: Filehandles
sections.content:
A filehandle is a per-server identifier for a filesystem object. It is opaque to the client, which MUST NOT interpret its contents but may compare two filehandles byte by byte. Equal filehandles MUST refer to the same file, though different ones may still name the same file, so comparison is only a performance hint.

NFS versions 2 and 3 used a separate MOUNT protocol (RPC program number 100005) to get the first filehandle. It had deficiencies in security and firewall use, so version 4 drops it. Clients instead start from one of two special filehandles: the ROOT filehandle, set with PUTROOTFH, is the conceptual root of the server's tree, and the PUBLIC filehandle, set with PUTPUBFH, is bound by the administrator to whatever object the server chooses.

Two kinds exist. A persistent filehandle keeps its value for the life of the object, even across server restarts, and a removed object yields NFS4ERR_STALE. A volatile filehandle can expire at points the server decides, and the server then returns NFS4ERR_FHEXPIRED. Volatile handles ease servers that cannot build persistent ones but add work for clients, which learn the type from a file attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: A filehandle is like a coat-check ticket. You do not know what the number means; you just hand it back and the server finds your coat. Some tickets stay good forever and some can expire.

sections.title: File Attributes
sections.content:
Version 3 used a fixed attribute structure that could not be extended and could not signal non-support. Version 4 splits attributes into three groups. Mandatory attributes are a deliberately small set every server must provide. Recommended attributes cover different filesystem types and environments, and a server should support as many as possible. Named attributes are opaque byte streams attached to a file or directory and meant for application data.

Mandatory and recommended attributes are identified by number. A client requests them by setting bits in a bitmap in GETATTR, and the reply carries a bitmap of what was returned. New ones can be added by a standards-track RFC that allocates a number and defines the encoding. Named attributes are reached through OPENATTR, which returns the filehandle of a hidden directory whose files are the attributes.

A notable recommended attribute is the Access Control List (ACL), which gives user and group access control beyond earlier versions. Owner and group are now strings rather than numeric uid and gid values. The lease_time attribute reports the lease duration, and the fs_locations attribute supports migration and replication.
sections.plainLanguage: Attributes are the facts on a file's label: how big it is, who owns it, when it changed. Some labels every file must have, some are optional, and you can also stick on your own notes.

sections.title: The Server Name Space
sections.content:
Servers rarely expose their whole filesystem, only chosen exports. In earlier versions, MOUNT handed out the root filehandle of each export, and an automounter's picture of the server's tree was static: a newly added export went unnoticed.

NFS version 4 presents all exports in one server name space. Gaps between real filesystems are bridged by a pseudo filesystem, a read-only view of the exported directories with its own fsid. A client browses from export to export with ordinary single-component LOOKUP and READDIR. Even when the root filesystem is exported, a pseudo filesystem is still needed: if / and /a/b are exported but /a is not, the server must bridge the gap.

A client notices a mount point crossing by a change in the fsid attribute. Since the pseudo filesystem is probably built dynamically, clients should expect its filehandles to be volatile. For security the server should apply the policy of a shared resource to its ancestors, so that hiding does not lock out legitimate clients.

Related is migration and replication through fs_locations, a list of server names and paths. For a migrated filesystem the old server returns NFS4ERR_MOVED (except for PUTFH and GETATTR), and the client reads fs_locations to redirect. Replication is expected mostly for read-only data.
sections.plainLanguage: The server shows you one tidy map of everything it shares. Where there are blank spots between shared folders, it paints in pretend folders so you can walk from one to the next.

sections.title: State, Leases and File Locking
sections.content:
Built-in locking makes the protocol stateful. The server owns the state, the client reports its view, and the client can detect inconsistency before changing a file. Locking and share reservations are acquired through the new OPEN operation, which combines the lookup, create and access steps of version 3, while LOOKUP remains for mapping a name to a filehandle without creating state.

A client first sends SETCLIENTID then SETCLIENTID_CONFIRM, supplying a verifier (to detect client reboots) and a unique id string. The server returns a short clientid. A new incarnation's registration immediately breaks the previous incarnation's leased state, but the server MUST NOT do so if the principal differs. Granted locks yield a stateid, which READ, WRITE and SETATTR then present; all zero bits mean no state, and the server must refuse I/O that conflicts with a share reservation or mandatory lock with NFS4ERR_LOCKED.

Lock requests carry sequence numbers, starting at zero for each lock owner, to get at-most-once behavior the RPC layer does not provide. State lives under a lease: one fixed duration for all state of a client, renewed by RENEW or implicitly by other operations such as READ. If the client fails to renew, the server may release its state.

After a server restart, clients re-establish locks during a grace period equal to the lease period. The server rejects normal READ, WRITE and non-reclaim lock requests with NFS4ERR_GRACE, unless it can prove no conflict is possible. Clients learn of the reboot from NFS4ERR_STALE_CLIENTID or NFS4ERR_STALE_STATEID.
sections.plainLanguage: The server is like a coat-room attendant who writes down who holds which hook. Each holder has a timer and must check in now and then. If the attendant faints and wakes up, everybody gets a short window to say which hooks were theirs before anyone new is served.

sections.title: Client Caching and Delegation
sections.content:
The protocol does not provide distributed cache coherence, as earlier versions did not. It defines a limited set of guarantees so locks and share reservations work despite client caching. Attributes and directory information are cached for a client-chosen time, and file data validity is checked at open, with modified data written back at close.

The major addition is delegation. At OPEN, when no conflicting access exists, the server may give a client a read or write delegation. With a read delegation no other client can write the file; with a write delegation no other client can read or write it. The client can then service operations such as OPEN, CLOSE, LOCK, LOCKU, READ and WRITE locally. The goal is to avoid repeated revalidation when a file is used by one client or shared read-only.

A delegation is recallable. If another client makes a conflicting request, the server uses a callback to recall it. The holder flushes modified state and returns the delegation, and the conflicting request waits until the recall completes or the server revokes the delegation on timeout. Correct operation does not depend on callbacks, because they may fail through firewalls: the server tests the path with CB_NULL and delegates only when callbacks look usable. Clients must never assume a delegation will be granted.
sections.plainLanguage: If nobody else wants a library book, the server lets you keep it at your desk and read it as often as you like without asking again. If someone else asks for it, the server calls you and you hand it back.

sections.title: Minor Versions and Internationalization
sections.content:
The protocol evolves through minor versions. Each minor version must be documented in a standards-track RFC, and minor version zero is this RFC. The COMPOUND request carries the minor version. The rules include: procedures are not added or deleted, operations may be added to COMPOUND, new attributes are appended after the last documented one, and existing operation structures, attributes, operations and flag bits are not modified or deleted. A minor version may declare an operation mandatory to not implement.

For internationalization, names and other strings use UTF-8. Three string types are defined, utf8str_cs, utf8str_cis and utf8str_mixed, each with its own stringprep profile (RFC 3454). The profiles set the character repertoire (Unicode 3.2), mapping, normalization and prohibited output.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book lets new chapters be added later, but old pages may never be torn out, so older machines still understand newer ones. Names are written in a code that can hold letters from any language.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
NFS historically treated the whole client machine, identified by IP address, as the authenticated party, with AUTH_SYS naming the user. The RFC calls this easy to deploy but not safe. NFS version 4 therefore mandates support for end-to-end authentication in which a user mutually authenticates with a principal on the server, without exposing passwords or keys on the network. AUTH_SYS is neither mandatory nor recommended, so interoperability through it is not assured.

Skipping integrity protection leaves users open to an attacker who alters requests or replies. Two operations deserve it regardless of user choice. SECINFO should be protected, or an attacker could push the client toward a weaker mechanism. A GETATTR for fs_locations should be too: an attacker could forge NFS4ERR_MOVED and then redirect the client to a server the attacker controls. Because SETCLIENTID and SETCLIENTID_CONFIRM release client state, the principal must match the earlier use.

For IANA, a registry for named attributes is available (registration by Informational RFC), and a registry of ONC RPC network identifiers is seeded with tcp, udp, tcp6 and udp6.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of letting anyone who walks in with the right address take files, the server checks each person's real identity. Two especially important messages must be sealed so nobody can swap them en route.

data.title: COMPOUND layout
data.code:
request:
| tag | minorversion | numops | op + args | op + args | op + args | ...

reply:
| last status | tag | numres | status + op + results | ...
